△ Section on the Separate Description of the Four Auspicious Omens, Part Four. First, the omen of the sixfold earthquake of the great earth:
At that time, as soon as the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara had spoken this Great Cakra Dhāraṇī King, the great earth immediately shook in six ways.
The Great Wheel possesses two meanings: first, it turns to open the way to the sacred realm; second, it grinds away the dust of the mundane world.
Because it is that toward which all mantras converge, it is called the King of Mantras. The earthquake signifies the appearance of the subduing of calamities and the entry into principle.

To sway unsteadily is called "shaking" (dòng). To rise from below upward is called "arising" (qǐ). To suddenly leap upward is called "leaping up" (yǒng). To produce a deep, rumbling sound is called... [the sound].

"Shen" (trembling). To rouse the voice so as to awaken is called "roaring"; to produce a crashing resonance is called "striking. The first three [terms] refer to form; the latter three refer to sound.
Now, one term is designated for each of both sound and form. Within these six types, there are again three for each: simple movement is called "movement" (1);
the movement of the four continents is called "universal movement" (2); the movement of the trichiliocosm is called... [the third].
The third is the universal shaking; the remaining five are likewise, totaling eighteen kinds.

In terms of the Dharma, these symbolize the destruction of ignorance throughout the six stages of faith, abiding, practice, transference, and the grounds (*bhūmi*). △ Second, the auspicious sign of the celestial palaces being shaken.
All the celestial palaces, nāga palaces, yakṣa palaces, as well as the palaces of the gandharvas, asuras, kinnaras, and so forth, all began to spin;
those who relied upon them became bewildered, and all the obstructing māras saw their own palaces ablaze with flames,
none of whom were not struck with terror— including sentient beings of evil intent, wicked nāgas, malevolent ghosts, and yakṣas.
The rākṣasas all fall headlong;

this symbolizes the phase of subduing Māra and perfecting one's practice. "All existences" (sarvabhava) refers collectively to the locus of dependence. Briefly stated, there are the three realms of existence (*tribhava*):
namely, desire, form, and formlessness. Elaborately stated, there are twenty-five existences: namely, the four continents, the four evil destinies, and the six heavens of the desire realm.

This includes the Brahmā heavens, the four dhyānas, the four formless attainments (*ārūpya*), the non-conceptual beings (*asaṃjñin*), and the *anāgāmins*. The Sanskrit term for *deva* is translated here as "heaven" (*tian*);
because their pleasure and bodies are superior, they refer to the gods of the desire and form realms. The Sanskrit term for *nāga* is translated here as "dragon" (*long*).
He dwells in the Vajra Cave to the south of Mount Sumeru; he is the deity of worldly pleasures for the Lord of Devas (*devendra*).
He possesses the skill of brandishing and hurling the *pratyāṅga* banner. Asura is translated here as "Non-Deva," because they possess the fortune of devas but lack the virtue of devas;
they are also called "Not-Ugly" because the males are ugly while the females are beautiful. They are also said to be "Without Wine"; they gather flowers and ferment them in the ocean, and its flavor—

It does not change, for anger and envy have been vowed to be severed. Furthermore, there are differences among the four realms of existence: devas (born by transformation), humans (born from a womb), and animals (born from moisture).
As clarified in the *Śūraṅgama-sūtra*, the Kiṃnara—here translated as "Doubting Spirit"—resembles a human being but has a horn upon its head;
it is a deity of the Dharma-pleasures of the Heavenly Kings. Possessing the arts of stringed instruments, pipes, and singing, it dwells on the Ten Jewel Mountains.
Their bodies emit a wondrous fragrance. "Then celestial music was played" refers to the two classes of *garuḍas* and *mahoragas*.
*Garuḍa* means "Golden Winged One" (*jīngì*); the distance between its two wings is three million three hundred and sixty thousand *li*.
He is golden in color and radiant; he has a wish-fulfilling jewel upon his neck and takes dragons as his food. He constantly comes to dwell atop *campaka* trees.
*Mahoraga*: this is translated as "great-bellied crawler. Kumārajīva said: "Earth-dragon. Sengzhao said: [As above].

The Nāga deity’s palace is his dwelling place. As for those who are deluded by its rotations, when the *vidyā-mantra* of sovereign power manifests, even the empty space before them would collapse, let alone the lands and palaces.
A sutra says: "The lands of even a single mote of dust are all established through deluded and stubborn false imaginings.
When one person gives rise to true realization and returns to the source, this empty space of the ten directions is entirely shattered."
"Perished. Why would the land not tremble and split apart? In the language of India, *māra*; in the language of Qin, "one who can take away life.

Because he takes away the life of wisdom (*prajñājīvitendriya*). He is also called "the slayer," because he slays the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*). Or he is called "the evil one," because he abounds in greed, anger, and jealousy.
He is also translated as "the obstacle," because he creates hindrances for the practitioner. As for "those struck with alarm by the rising flames":
Wherever the Mantra of the Jewel-Wheel King reaches, the palaces of Pāpīyān spontaneously crumble. The *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* states:

"When you practitioners of dhyāna—bodhisattvas and arhats—have attained mastery in the mind, it shall be profoundly still in that very place. When the Māra kings, ghosts, and spirits see their palaces collapse and crack for no apparent reason, there are none who are not struck with terror.
Sentient beings of evil intent point to the ninety-five kinds of external [paths]..."
The Way extends even to the icchantikas and those who have severed their roots of goodness.
Rākṣasas—meaning "the swift," or alternatively "the fearsome"—are ghosts that devour the vital essence of humans. As for those who have all fallen into ruin:

when the Lotus Heart Mantra is expounded, the goblins and spirits who cling to these worldly defilements will naturally be crushed and extinguished within wondrous enlightenment. The Sūtra says: *Śamatha*.
The central awakening-consciousness analyzes and discerns; the powerful ghosts and spirits lose their souls and flee.

That these twelve—comprising both the primary and secondary [realms]—are joined together represents the subduing of the inverted delusions of the twelve classes of beings within the twelve sense bases (*āyatana*).
△ Third, the auspicious sign of the three miserable realms being freed from suffering.
All sentient beings suffering within the hells are entirely freed from their suffering and attain rebirth in the heavens;
this symbolizes the characteristics of the teachings of love and reverence. The hells beneath the earth are called "earth-hells" (*bhūmi-naraka*). *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*.

These hells are categorized as "intermittent" (*sāntara*) for those of lighter offenses and "uninterrupted" (*ānantarya*) for those of heavier offenses. For those who have been summoned by the gravest of rebellious acts,
the Great Wheel Mantra King proclaims that their karmic retributions across the three miserable realms shall be completely extinguished—

just as those in the Avīci Hell are uplifted to the Tuṣita Heaven by the light of the Śākyamuni Tathāgata— or as ten thousand fish were liberated from rebirth upon hearing the mantra of the Elder Jalavāhana.

The Trāyastriṃśa Heaven; hence it is said that by leaving suffering one is born in heaven. In terms of the Dharma, this symbolizes that by relying on the three kinds of prajñā, one transforms the three kinds of evil karma of sentient beings and accomplishes the three kinds of virtuous karma of the Tathāgata. △ Fourth, correlating this with the auspicious omen of the rain-offering from the previous assembly.
At that time, within the assembly, before the World-Honored One, a rain of precious flowers and precious ornaments fell from the sky,
while celestial music was played in the air, producing various sounds as they presented extensive offerings.

This indicates the signs of increasing merit and attaining the fruit. "Jewel flowers" refers to the *māndārava* (here translated as "pleasing," or "white flower") and the *mañjūṣaka* (here translated as "soft," or "red flower"), and so forth.
As for the mantras, because they are formed by the binding of the body of samādhi, they evoke offerings of flowers and precious implements.

"Refers to garments, parasols, canopies, banners, pennants, garlands, nets, and so forth. Since the mantra is formed from the aggregate of ethical discipline (*śīla-skandha*), it brings about the enjoyment of material offerings.
'Various sounds' refers to the Truths, the Bases of Mindfulness, the Factors of Enlightenment, the Ten Powers, the Four Fearlessnesses, and so forth.

Since the mantra is formed from the aggregate of wisdom (*prajñā-skandha*), it brings about the enjoyment of the Dharma. Those who recite and those who uphold [the mantra] increase the merit and bliss of the three bodies: the Dharma-body, the Transformation-body, and the Reward-body."
One attains the fruit of the three types of bodhi through the true nature, skillful means, and actual wisdom;

this serves as the precursor. Regarding the extensive presentation of offerings, there are two kinds: first, material offerings, also called ritual offerings; these are further divided into two: (1) internal offerings, such as the three fruits and food;
and (2) Dharma offerings, also called rational offerings. As the *Chapter on Vows and Practices* states: "Among all forms of offering, the Dharma offering..."

Supreme. This refers to the offering of practicing according to the teachings, the offering of benefiting sentient beings, the offering of not abandoning the bodhisattva’s deeds, and the offering of not departing from the bodhicitta.
In terms of the Dharma, this signifies the breaking of the two kinds of cognitive obstructions and the realization of the two-fold transformation of the basis (āśraya-parāvṛtti) of all Buddhas.
△ Third, praising and demonstrating the upholding of the Dharma to accomplish practice, in three parts. First, the praise.
May this seal cause the assembly to arise and fulfill their aspirations.
At that time, the World-Honored One, with a sublime and beautiful voice, praised the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara, saying:
"Excellent, excellent, Avalokiteśvara! What you have proclaimed is a great king of mantras, truly difficult to encounter, which is able to cause the multitude..."
When born, one’s prayers are fulfilled and one obtains great rewards.

Its various sounds are all complete and may be called "beautiful," like the voice of the celestial maiden Suvaktrā; it does not deviate from the multitude and may be called "sublime," like the speech and tone of Brahmā.

Furthermore, its conformity to the truth may be called "beautiful," and its accordance with the capacities of beings may be called "sublime. Excellent! This is the praise for the mantra that has been spoken.
This is as with all intentions. Below, "Excellent! is a praise for the fulfillment of the vow to benefit sentient beings and bring all fruits to completion.
If one can practice and maintain this, the merit will not be in vain. △ Second, the extensive demonstration that all should rely on the teaching and practice accordingly, in two parts.
First, the demonstration of the ritual method for reciting the mantra. Part one: the general heading.
"If there are any ritual methods for reciting this mantra, I shall now explain them.
Although the mantra is like the udumbara flower, like a *maṇi* jewel, like celestial nectar, and like a treasury of rare treasures," if...

It would not be in accordance with the Dharma, nor would it achieve any benefit; therefore, the Buddha’s teaching is invoked as a pretext to demonstrate that there is no error. △ Second, the detailed explanation has two parts.
First, the direct instruction to maintain the mantra with single-mindedness.
If there are sons or daughters of good family— whether bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, or upāsikās—
who resolve their minds to seek the manifest retribution of this life, they should single-mindedly receive and uphold this mantra.

"Virtuous sons and daughters" refers to all those with pure faith; this includes everyone within the eight classes of beings and the six realms of existence who have seen, heard, or rejoiced in [the teaching].
"Bhikṣu" is a Sanskrit term for a type of grass in the Western lands (India). Because it possesses five virtues, it is used as a metaphor:

first, its nature is soft and supple, symbolizing how the Saṃgha can subdue both body and speech so they do not become coarse or wild; second, its trailing vines spread out to the sides, serving as a metaphor...

1. The Sangha can transmit the Dharma and deliver sentient beings in an uninterrupted succession; this illustrates how the Sangha’s virtuous conduct is continuous and unceasing. 2. The third is that its fragrance is heard afar;

this is a metaphor for the Sangha’s fragrant precepts and virtues being known by all. 3. The fourth is that it can cure pain; this is a metaphor for the Sangha’s ability to sever the poisonous harm of afflictions so they do not arise.
4. The fifth is that it does not turn its back on the sun; this is a metaphor for the Sangha constantly facing the Buddha-sun and the radiance of wisdom. This concludes the enumeration.
The *pravrajita bhikṣu* is an ordained monk; the *pravrajitā bhikṣuṇī* is an ordained nun.

The *upāsaka*—translated into Chinese as "near-attendant male"—is a layman who observes the five precepts. The *upāsikā*—translated into Chinese as "near-attendant female"—is a laywoman who observes the five precepts.
To "arouse the mind" and "aspire" refers to making a vow. "Retribution in this life" (*dṛṣṭadharmavedanīya*) encompasses all wholesome deeds, both mundane and supramundane.

"Wondrous cause and effect" means to distinguish this from seeking to repay past kindnesses or plotting for future retribution. "Receiving" (*shou*) refers to the conceptualizations of the mental consciousness;

"retaining" (*chi*) refers to the recitation and practice of body and speech. There are two types of single-mindedness: first, single-mindedness of the event (*shi*), which means focusing the mind with total concentration, without the slightest interruption;
second, single-mindedness of principle (*li*), which means awakening to this mindful mind such that subject and object, grasping and what is grasped, are severed and its sharpness is realized.

Regarding the principle of wisdom: those of dull faculties maintain [the practice] through the matter of receiving [instruction]; those of middling faculties apply to both types. △ Next, to clarify the ritual for recitation:
when one wishes to receive and maintain [the mantra], one need not inquire about the auspiciousness of the days, months, or stars, nor is it necessary to separately observe fasts or precepts.
By bathing and wearing clean robes, simply restraining the mind and reciting this without ceasing, one’s hundreds of thousands of desires will be fulfilled.

This King of Mantras is the time when the Sun of the Yellow Path and the Star of the Purple Tenuity arrive; it transforms the inauspicious into the auspicious and brings forth blessings even when encountering calamities.
Therefore, there is no need to inquire about the auspiciousness or inauspiciousness of the day or the stars. This mantra-heart is itself the Bodhisattva’s Ground of the Mind.

Regarding precepts: wherever one goes, they naturally constitute the observance of the fast and its prohibitions; thus, there is no need to rely on the practice of observing the *śīla* on specific monthly fasting days.
This secret mantra is the water of *dharmatā* that washes and cleanses the field of the body; thus, it does not depend on ritual bathing, for all are equally pure.

This clarifying mantra is the garment of liberation that fully covers shame and modesty; thus, it does not require washing, for it is naturally fresh and clean. However, this is because of the practitioner’s cessation [of afflictions].
Furthermore, while external decorum may permit occasional lapses, internal virtue must never transgress its boundaries; thus, the three karmas are essential.

Should any evil spirits, malevolent deities, wicked dragons, or ferocious beasts cause harm to the people, or if there are those with cruel hearts who poison others, slander the Triple Gem, destroy the practice of mantra, or act with lack of loyalty and filial piety to create obstacles—within both the mundane and supramundane laws of cause and effect—one must swiftly [act].

Fulfilling merit and wisdom, they suddenly perfect the truths, conditions, perfections, and practices; transcending the three *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas* and ascending to the ten stages (*bhūmi*), they attain the five vehicles' superior positions and the two fruits of the transformation of the basis (*āśraya-parāvṛtti*). Regarding all such various matters, there is nothing they do not fulfill through their aspirations;
thus it is said that "hundreds of thousands of matters are all accomplished. One should only fear reciting the words while failing to collect the mind, or being diligent for but a moment.

I have long held you in reverence, yet have not obtained a spiritual response; perhaps it has not yet been time. △ Second, a detailed explanation of the efficacy of the mantra recitation, in two parts.
First, to manifest its supreme excellence:
there is no other mantra of clear wisdom whose power can equal that of this King of Wish-Fulfilling Mantras.
The King of Mantras that Fulfills Wishes is the mother of all Buddhas and the father of Bodhisattvas; it is the root of heaven and earth and the foundation of all spiritual powers.

It is like the seal of a Wheel-Turning King, the decree of Brahmā, the banner of Śakra, the edict of a sovereign, the sword of Vajra, the white ox-cart, the sandalwood from the Ocean Treasury and the Elephant Treasury, and the medicinal pellets of the Flower Treasury and Pure Treasury.
Its power is supreme and beyond compare. Yet, sentient beings in the six realms are destitute of merit and wisdom;
being separated from the Buddha of Great Power and the Dharma that severs suffering, the Bodhisattva gives rise to a heart of great compassion and proclaims this subtle and most excellent mantra.
Any person who is able to receive and uphold it will likewise possess power that has no equal. △ Next, the divine [nature] is explained.
The three powers: first, causing the worldly mind’s aspirations to be fulfilled as desired; second, first clarifying what is to be aspired to. First, the general [explanation]:
"Therefore, one should first eliminate all karmic obstacles of sin; subsequently, one will be able to accomplish all undertakings."

Malignity and rebellion are called "sins" (*pāpa*). Obstruction and interference are called "hindrances" (*āvaraṇa*). The retribution of sin is like frost and snow; the luminous mantra is like the sun and boiling water.

Calamities and hindrances are like ashes and sand; the wheel-mantra is like a fierce wind. Therefore, it is said that [the mantra] "removes" them. That which has not yet been accomplished is called "matters" (*kriyā*);

that which has already been formed is called "karma" (*karman*). Joyful matters are like a charred wick; the divine mantra is like fragrant oil. Auspicious karma is like a ship; the secret mantra is...
It is like going with the current; hence it is said that "it is accomplished. △ Second, the specific [effects] has two parts. First, it extinguishes past karmic retributions.

It can also eliminate the grave offenses of the five heinous acts that lead to rebirth in the Avīci Hell, and it can utterly eradicate all suffering from illness, such that one attains complete recovery.

In Sanskrit, *avīci* is translated as "uninterrupted" (*wújiàn*). According to the *Abhidharmakośa-śāstra*, regarding the attainment of the fruit [of retribution], the five factors—time, suffering, lifespan, and physical form—are all uninterrupted.

Among the hells, this refers to the most severe fruit. The five heinous crimes (*pañcānantarya*) are: killing one's father, killing one's mother, [killing an arhat, shedding the blood of a Buddha, and causing schism in the Sangha].
Killing an Arhat, shedding the blood of a Buddha, and disrupting the Saṃgha that performs the *karmavācanā* and turns the wheel of Dharma are causes for the most grave offenses.

Since mantras act as a pardon for these hells, it is said they "eliminate" them. Furthermore, various illnesses and calamities that entangle one are likewise due to the lingering debts of past misdeeds;
since mantras serve as a skilled physician and wondrous medicine, it is said they "cure and extinguish" them. Question: Regarding the crimes of hell and the offenses of rebellion...
...and sickness is an obstacle. Even if these are removed, how could auspicious undertakings not achieve success? Answer: Only when hell is extinguished do human and celestial affairs proceed;
only when sickness is removed do meritorious and joyful karmas succeed. The text implies this by way of shadowing [the meaning], and thus it is not explicitly stated.
The following sections follow this pattern. △ Second, the extinction of present retributive offenses, in two parts: first, the removal of karmic offenses.
It is capable of destroying all heavy karmas.
Grave acts of parricide and rebellion are the cause for rebirth in hell; middling acts of parricide and rebellion are the cause for rebirth as a hungry ghost;

minor acts of parricide and rebellion are the cause for rebirth as an animal. If even such grave offenses can be destroyed, how much more so those that are light and small? Karma is like withered grass; the mantra is like—
A fierce fire; upon encountering it, everything is reduced to ashes without remainder. △ Second, the transformation of karmic retribution, in nine parts.

First, malarial fevers: all those with feverish illnesses—whether occurring by day or night, or as quotidian, tertian, or quartan malaria, or afflictions such as wind, bile, phlegm, and chronic wasting—will be cured simply by reciting this mantra.
Mantras can cure the seven types of illnesses—fever, malaria, wind, jaundice, phlegm, and those of the three *tridoṣas*—because they are the talismans for longevity.
As the Sūtra says: "If you wish to attain the ground of immortality, you should wear the talisman of longevity. The talisman of longevity is none other than the Dharma of the Three Vehicles.
2. Poison from Malevolent Spirits (*gudu*).
If there are others who practice sorcery, bewitchment, or the use of poisons, all shall be completely extinguished without remainder.
"Sorcery" (dǎo) refers to incantations and curses. In Sanskrit, it is *miliduō wéituóluó* (mṛtyu-vedala), which here means "Lord of Wondrous Goodness. Regarding "sorcery" (dǎo):

the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* states that those encountered in the darkness who manifest forms are called *yàn guǐ* (suffocating ghosts); they are malevolent spirits that cause confusion and delusion. [End of] Scripture.
It is said: those of superior grade are possessed by spirits; those of middling grade, by *yāksas* and *rākṣasas*; and those of inferior grade, by various demons and malevolent persons.

"Poison" (*gū*) refers to the worms within the belly and to poisons derived from gold, silver, plants, and trees—meaning that one administers these various poisonous charms (*gū*) to the physical body, clothing, and food.
In Sanskrit, this is called *milindu-gāthaka*, which here means "Master of Good Qualities. As for "poisonous charms" (*gū*), [it refers to the aforementioned].

The Sūtra says: "When insects encounter one another and take form, they are called *gudu* (poisonous spirits). One who can extinguish them through mantras does so because of the ambrosial nectar (*amṛta-rasa*).
The Sūtra says: 'For example, if a person drinks the ambrosial nectar, no sentient beings or things can cause them harm.
If one constantly maintains this, their body will ultimately remain unchanging and indestructible. △ Third, abscesses and pains."
Suppose that all manner of abscesses, goiters, malignant sores, scabies, carbuncles, and ringworms were to cover his entire body, including the eyes, ears, nose, tongue,
lips, mouth, teeth, throat, crown of the head, brain, chest, ribs, heart, abdomen, waist, back, hands, feet, head, and face;
and that he suffered from aching in his limbs and joints, hemiplegia, abdominal distension with hard masses, and indigestion, starting from the head...
It is sufficient that every ailment and suffering shall be healed without exception.
When the six bowels are disharmonized, abscesses arise; when the five viscera are disordered, carbuncles arise—these being swellings and tumors.
Of the eleven kinds of maladies and twenty-three kinds of pains, there are none that it does not cure. This incantation is the medicine of immortality, the elixir for prolonging life.
Therefore, the Sūtra says: "For example, it is like a person who holds the 'Good Vision' (Sudarśana) medicine and is able to cure all existing ailments.
Or again, it is like a person who ingests an elixir of longevity, remaining forever robust, neither aging nor emaciated. △ Fourth, the ghosts and spirits.
If there are yakṣas, rākṣasas, vināyakas, evil ghosts, spirits, or any who commit wicked deeds, none shall find an opportunity to cause harm.
*Vināyaka* here means "pig-head," and *yaka* means "elephant-nose"; these are the names of two classes of spirits. "Shall not find an opportunity" means they shall have no chance to act.
This is because the mantra is the vajra of the Heavenly Emperor. The *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* states:
"Just as the Heavenly King Śakra wields the vajra to subdue all asuras, ghosts, and spirits. The *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* states:
"By holding this mantra-heart, Piṇāyaka and all other evil ghost-kings shall all acknowledge its profound kindness and constantly provide protection. △ Fifth, disasters and calamities.
Furthermore, no swords, staves, weapons, arrows, water, fire, poisons, evil winds, rain, hail, enemies, thieves, or robbers can reach their bodies.
Water, fire, and wind constitute the three calamities; the remainder are the eight difficulties. None of these can affect them. This mantra is like a *maṇi* jewel.
The Crown. It is like the *abhaya-guṭikā* (pill of fearlessness). A sutra states: "When Śakra wears the maṇi crown, it outshines all other hosts of devas.
When a nāga king wears the maṇi crown, he remains far removed from all fear of enemies.
When a human obtains the *abhaya-guṭikā* medicine, they are freed from the five terrors: namely, fire cannot burn them, water cannot drown them, and blades cannot wound them."
Poisons cannot strike him; smoke cannot suffocate him. △ Regarding the six calamitous thieves:
neither royal thieves nor any other sudden deaths come to inflict harm upon him.
Royal thieves constitute two of the nine types of sudden death; none of the various great or small calamities can cause him injury. This mantra is a method for concealing one's form.
Because it is the method for liberation. As the Sūtra says: "For example, suppose there is a person who obtains a spell for making oneself invisible;
neither humans nor non-humans can see them. Furthermore, suppose a person obtains añjana and applies it to their eyes;

though they walk among people, no one sees them. Again, suppose a person obtains a medicinal recipe for liberation; they will never encounter untimely calamities. Furthermore, they obtain the juice of ālambā."
By using it to anoint the body, both body and mind will possess full capability. △ Seventh, regarding insects and beasts:
various evil dreams, vipers, snakes, scorpions, lizards, centipedes, spiders, and all other malevolent venomous creatures—tigers, wolves, and lions—will be entirely unable to cause harm.
The *luán* snake is a black snake; its venom is so potent that it does not bite but merely inhales it. The *fú* snake is a viper. The scorpion and the centipede—these two sting if touched.
The *shǒugōng* is a gecko; the *bǎizú* is a millipede. To recite mantras so that they cannot cause harm means to empower them with incantations.
Because of the dragon-jewel (nāga-maṇi) and because of the mahā-śaṅkha medicine. As the Sūtra says: "If a person obtains a dragon-jewel, no dragons or snakes can cause them harm.
If a person carries the mahā-śaṅkha medicine, as soon as the snakes and insects smell its fragrance, they will all flee far away."
△ 8. The Array of the Eight Armies:
All military engagements and battle arrays shall achieve victory.
Because this mantra is like the precious [jewel] of the Celestial Malla General, one attains victory within the midst of battle arrays. △ 9.
Regarding official litigation:
if there are disputes or lawsuits, they can likewise be reconciled.
Because the mantra is like the imperial decree of the Emperor and the Seal of Eternal Joy, it is able to harmonize private disputes and resolve official litigation. △ Next.
The Bright One is able to uphold it.
If one recites it once, all the aforementioned vows will be fulfilled according to one's wishes.
Regarding "the aforementioned": first, it eliminates all present light and heavy karmic obstacles; next, the nine [subsequent sections] bring about accomplishment.
The present activities that transform all suffering into happiness comprise ten types. This mantra is like a wish-fulfilling jewel, providing for all who are destitute.
This mantra is like a vase of merit, satisfying the hearts of all sentient beings.
This mantra is like a wish-fulfilling tree, able to rain down all manner of ornaments. This mantra is like a hidden treasure, from which wealth emerges without exhaustion. This mantra is like...
A bright mirror universally manifests all forms and images; thus, even one recitation fulfills everything completely, let alone two, seven, or up to forty-nine recitations.
△ Second, causing the worldly mind’s vows to be fulfilled as desired, in two parts: first, clarifying the capacity for upholding [the name].

If one recites this one hundred and eight times every day, manifesting diligence daily without retreating—rather than being like those who practice for ten days and neglect it for one—the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* states:
"It is like drilling wood to seek fire; if one stops repeatedly before the fire emerges, the heat will cease and the fire will be extinguished. So too is it with those who are indolent. Therefore...

On that day, recite them in succession; do not allow for any interruption. The "one hundred and eight" symbolizes the breaking of the one hundred and eight views and afflictions, thereby accomplishing the one hundred and eight Dharma-gates.
△ Next, the seventh section clarifies the vows: first, fulfilling all requests.
Then he saw Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva saying: "O son of good family, do not fear! Whatever vow you seek, I shall grant it all to you.
Regarding "granting everything":
this refers to the four fruits of the śrāvaka, the five stages of the bodhisattva, the three knowledges, the six supernormal powers, the two emptinesses, and the ten [powers].
They bestow all powers, bodhi, and nirvana, granting everything that is prayed for or sought. △ Second, manifesting the Buddha-body:
Amitābha Buddha manifests his own body.
In the Sanskrit language it is *Amitābha*; here it is translated as "Immeasurable Life" (*Wúliàngshòu*) and also as "Immeasurable Light" (*Wúliàngguāng*).
The mantra is the awakened mind of the Tathāgata; by reciting it, one becomes a successor to the Buddha’s awakening. The former belongs to the cause, while this belongs to the fruit;
together they constitute the gateway that thoroughly encompasses both cause and effect. △ Second, beholding the Land of Bliss.
One also sees the various adornments of the World of Ultimate Bliss as described extensively in the sutra.
Because it is free from all suffering, it is named "Ultimate Bliss" (Sukhāvatī). It is the dwelling place of Avalokiteśvara and Amitābha. Regarding the various adornments:
one sees the Land of Ultimate Bliss adorned with the seven treasures, with jeweled grounds, jeweled ponds, and rows of jeweled trees, [surrounded by] the various devas.
Jeweled curtains cover it from above, and nets of various jewels fill the void of space. The flowing waters, radiant light, wild ducks, geese, and mandarin ducks all proclaim the Dharma.
This refers to the *Sukhāvatīvyūha-sūtra*, the *Amitābha-sūtra*, and the *Amitāyurdhyāna-sūtra*.

As for the dhāraṇī, it is the realm of the joy of *dharmatā*; by upholding it, one spontaneously attains its enjoyment. In contrast to what precedes and follows, this is called the "basis. Taken together, they are named [the *Dhāraṇī-śambara-rāja-sūtra*].
This is the Gate of Mutual Interpenetration between the Primary and the Secondary [Realms]. △ Fourth, regarding the beholding of the Bodhisattvas:
one also sees the multitude of Bodhisattvas in the Land of Ultimate Bliss.

The *Sukhāvatīvyūha Sūtra* states: "In that land, there are two Bodhisattvas who occupy the position of succession to Buddhahood: the first is named Avalokiteśvara, and the second is named Mahāsthāmaprāpta."
Śrī-garbha, furthermore, the number of other bodhisattvas and śrāvakas is immeasurable. The Buddha told Maitreya:
"In this world, sixty-seven billion non-retrogressive bodhisattvas will be reborn in that land. Bodhisattvas of minor practice are beyond calculation.
From the great bodhisattvas who have been reborn in the fourteen buddha-lands of other directions, they are exceedingly numerous and incalculable."
Those who are now able to see [this] do so because, within this *dhāraṇī*, the myriad practices of the Bodhisattvas are entirely subsumed.
△ Fifth, beholding all Buddhas:
they also behold all Buddhas of the ten directions.

This mantra-heart gives birth to all Buddhas. By means of this mantra-heart, the Buddhas of the ten directions attain perfect enlightenment, subdue Māra, turn the wheel of Dharma, and bestow predictions of enlightenment.
Therefore, within the hundred and eight recitations, one is able to see all Buddhas in every thought-moment.
The former is the attendant; this is the principal figure. Together, they are called the "Gate of the Perfect Clarity of Principal and Attendant.
△ Sixth, contemplating the abode of the Sage: one also sees the mountain of Potalaka, the dwelling place of the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara.

Regarding the "place of residence": this refers to the place where the Bodhisattva manifests his transformation-body. *Potalaka* here is translated as "sea-island" (*hai-dao*) and also as "small white-flowered tree.
This mountain abounds in such trees, and because their fragrance is perceived from afar, the *Xiyu ji* (Records of the Western Regions) states:
To the south of Mount Trāyastriṃśa, there is a stone celestial palace, which is the dwelling place where the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara dwells.
The *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* states: "Upon the sea there is a mountain, inhabited by many sages and worthies; composed of various jewels, it is exceedingly pure.
Flowers, fruits, and groves of trees fill it everywhere, and springs, streams, ponds, and pools are all fully present. Therein dwells the heroic man, Avalokiteśvara."

"For the benefit of sentient beings, he dwells upon this mountain. The main body of the prose states: "On its western side, amidst the crags and valleys, one sees springs and streams winding and reflecting light;
the forests are lush and verdant, and fragrant herbs, soft and supple, cover the ground in a clockwise spiral.
There, the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara sits in the full lotus posture (*paryaṅka*) upon a diamond-jewel rock, surrounded by immeasurable bodhisattvas, all likewise seated upon jewels."
Śīla (the Stone). They respectfully surrounded him and he proclaimed for them the Dharma of Great Compassion, causing them to embrace all sentient beings.
Those who see it now likewise perceive that the mantra is the mountain of the Bodhisattva’s merit and the ocean of great compassion.
△ Seventh, obtaining a pure body.
One immediately attains purity of one's own body.

This "purity of one's own body" refers to the purification of the six sense faculties (*ṣaḍindriya-viśuddhi*) within the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*. Its stage corresponds to the ten levels of faith (*daśa-śraddhā*).

It is by means of the six sense faculties being fully gathered and pure mindfulness succeeding one another that this fruit is accomplished. The mantra issues from the mind of True Suchness (*tathatā-citta*) and the Dharma-nature (*dharmatā*).
The "Flowing Body" (Shinryū): Reciting this ensures that one's body is not left unpurified. While the preceding [practice] was for others, this is for oneself;
together they are called the "Entrance Gate of Gathering Self and Others. △ Third, causing worldly and world-transcending aspirations to be fulfilled as desired.
They shall always be respectfully honored and supported by kings, dukes, high ministers, and counselors, and be beloved and revered by all people.

In whatever place they are born, they shall not enter a mother’s womb but be born through transformation from a lotus flower, endowed with all marks of excellence. In every place of birth, they shall always attain the recollection of past lives;
from this day forth until they attain Buddhahood, they shall never fall into the evil realms and shall always be born in the presence of the Buddhas.
First, in this present life, one receives the honor and offerings of kings and ministers, gains the respect and affection of fellow beings, and fulfills all worldly aspirations.
Second, in future lives, one possesses the marks of a superior being and attains the supernormal knowledge of recollecting past lives, thereby fulfilling all supramundane aspirations.

Third, from now until the time of perfect enlightenment, one is always born in the presence of the Buddhas of the ten directions; these collectively manifest that all mundane and supramundane vows are fully realized.
This is the meaning. Because the mantra is like a *maṇi* jewel, a treasure-store jar, it can thus accord with one's vows and intentions.
△ Third, the conclusion and admonition, instructing the practitioner to have sincere faith and not doubt.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara addressed the Buddha, saying:

"World-Honored One, regarding this Candana-hṛdaya-cakra-dhāraṇī as I have explained it, if any bhikṣu, bhikṣuṇī, upāsaka, or upāsikā should recollect it with a sincere heart and be able to uphold it, they will certainly attain accomplishment; they need only have deep faith."
A doubt arises (that there may be further medicinal methods within this treasury that have been concealed and not brought forth).
This is the *Candana-citta-cakra* (Sandalwood Heart-Wheel), an abbreviated title; its full name is *Candana-maṇi-citta-ratna-cakra-rāja* (Sandalwood Maṇi Heart-Jewel Wheel King).

To be "sincere" means not deceiving oneself internally and not deceiving others externally; it refers to being truthful and without falsehood. "Heart-mind" (*citta*) refers to the sincerity of one's intention.
The body is the sincerity of the person; the tongue is the sincerity of the mouth. When the three karmas are reverent and respectful, one’s hundredfold aspirations will surely be fulfilled.
Faith is the foremost of virtues and the leader of all merits. The *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* says: "Faith is the source of the Way and the mother of merit;
it nurtures all roots of goodness. Faith enables one to reach the stage of the Tathāgata; faith is the indestructible seed of merit."
Faith can increase the most supreme wisdom; faith can manifest all Buddhas. The *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* asks: "What is faith?

Its nature is a pure mind characterized by profound acceptance, delight, and aspiration toward reality, virtue, and capability. Its function is to counteract lack of faith and to take pleasure in the wholesome.
Furthermore, there are briefly three distinctions of faith: first, faith in real existence, which refers to [faith] regarding all phenomena..."

1. Because of profound faith and acceptance regarding the reality of things and principles; 2. Because of faith in the possession of virtues, meaning because of profound faith and acceptance regarding the true and pure virtues of the Triple Gem;

3. Because of faith in the possession of capability, meaning because of profound faith in the power of all mundane and supramundane virtues to be attained and accomplished, thereby giving rise to aspiration.
By means of these antidotes, one counteracts the mind of non-belief and develops affection [for the Dharma].

One delights in realizing and cultivating mundane and supramundane virtues. Now, this faith is also threefold: first, faith that the mantra possesses great divine power and will certainly fulfill one's wishes;
second, faith that the Buddha’s words are not false and that by relying upon them, one's heart's desires will be attained;

third, faith that the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara, endowed with great compassion and vows, constantly bestows protection and support. Furthermore, within the *Arousing Faith Sūtra*, before the Three Jewels—
Furthermore, there is one root of faith: namely, the joyful recollection of the *tathatā* (suchness) dharma.
Now, through this faith, one realizes that one’s own mind is the Buddha and that one’s own mind creates the Buddha. Mantras arise from the mind, and the fruit is attained by the mind.
Apart from my *tathatā*-mind, not a single dharma exists as a conceptual construct. As stated in the *Brahmajāla Sūtra*: "You shall become a Buddha; I have already [become one]."
One shall attain Buddhahood. One should maintain such faith. When the precepts are fully perfected, this is precisely faith in the fundamental dharma of *tathatā* (suchness).
Once the fourfold faith arises, all aspirations will be fulfilled; this is the essential task of upholding [the Dharma]. Therefore, it is exhorted:
"Doubt alone is the basis of evil and the root of transgression. As Confucius said: "If a person lacks faith, they are no better than a beast."
One knows that it is possible; yet there are three types of doubt. First, doubting that one is not a suitable vessel. Second, doubting that the teacher has erred regarding oneself.
Third, doubting that the Dharma is not in accordance with principle. According to the specific teaching, these are: first, doubting that the mantra lacks spiritual efficacy;

second, doubting that the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas will not necessarily grant their protection; third, doubting that one’s own karmic obstacles are too heavy to be a vessel for the Dharma. Third, [doubting] while in...
[The practitioner] harbors [this intent], yet their progress in seeking it is not vigorous. Even mundane cause and effect are difficult to achieve;

how much more so the supramundane? Therefore, the admonition states: "One must not give rise to this [negligence]. These exhortations serve as the final model for Bodhisattvas. (A note at the end of the text states:

"Regarding 'further medicinal methods,' this refers to the detailed instructions on the methods of recitation and the methods of harmonious joy found in both the translations by Śikṣānanda and Amoghavajra. Those who require them should consult these. △ Fourth, the conclusion and exhortation to verify through personal experience.
Regarding the two [sections] on the realization of the fruit: first, the entrustment to realize and verify it, which has two parts. The first praises and reveals its miraculous efficacy.
At that time, the World-Honored One praised the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara, saying: "Excellent, excellent!
You, whose great compassion is immeasurable, are able to proclaim this subtle and wondrous *cintāmaṇi-cakra-dhāraṇī* method. Within Jambudvīpa, there are those..."
If sentient beings give rise to the aspiration and recite it aloud, they shall immediately obtain personal verification.

First, the "Excellent! (Sādhu) is praised: if one maintains it, it is accomplished; if one does not maintain it, it is not accomplished. It is like sandalwood: when near, it is fragrant; when far, it is not.
These words are not deceptive. Next, the "Excellent! is praised again: if one has faith, one approaches [success]; if one lacks faith, one does not.

It is as follows: it is like the water-purifying jewel; when thrown into water, the water becomes clear, and when not thrown, it does not. These words are true. Bestowing immeasurable bliss is called "Great Compassion" (mahāmaitrī).
Its spiritual resonance being unfathomable is called "Subtle" (sūkṣma). Its divine response being inconceivable is called "Wondrous" (miao).
Jambū is translated here as "Superior Gold. It is the name of a tree. In the forest there is a river; the juice from the tree fruits falls into the bottom of the river.
Dyeing sand to appear as gold, its color is reddish-yellow with streaks of purple flame; only in Jambudvīpa does this tree exist, hence it is taken as the name for this continent.
This is a personal verification and attainment of the spiritual efficacy of reciting mantras. Question:
Although a Bodhisattva does not fail to manifest in any land, they have a particular affinity with Sahā [World]. Why, in this context, is Jambudvīpa alone specifically mentioned? Answer: One.
"Among the ten billion sets of four great continents (*cāturdvīpaka*), one is cited to represent the rest. Second, among the three thousand [world systems], only Jambudvīpa is supreme.
First, a Tathāgata descends to be born there; second, the devas vow to come there; third, the Prajñā-pāramitā scriptures exist there; fourth, one is able to sever lustful desire;
fifth, one recognizes wholesome and unwholesome thoughts; sixth, one possesses courageous diligence. Of these six, the first three..."

The conditions are superior. The latter three causes are superior; since the other three continents cannot equal them, he specifically mentions the beings of Jambudvīpa to encourage their development.
△ Second, the instruction to realize through direct experience.
Relying on my teaching, you must repeatedly and diligently exhort and instruct all sentient beings so that they may attain realization;
manifest your form for them and do not disobey my command, and I shall rejoice in your efforts.

"Repeatedly" means that one does not distinguish between years or days, nor does one consider whether one's faculties are sharp or dull, nor does one select based on whether the teaching is small or great, nor differentiate according to whether the principle is partial or complete.
"Diligently applying oneself" refers to making progress; it means causing those who have not yet planted roots of goodness to plant them.
He causes those who have already planted [seeds] to grow; he causes those who are not yet matured to reach maturity; and he causes those who are already matured to attain liberation.
He exhorts them through practice, rouses them through fruition, reveals the truth through principle, and instructs them through teaching.

He manifests his own body and speech to empower them, so that they may realize the principle, the fruit, the verification, the teaching, and the practice. This is the Imperial Edict of the Son of Heaven.

It is said: "The Edict. The instructions of the Dharma King are equivalent to the commands of a sovereign; therefore, it says, "Do not disobey my edict. "To follow" means to accord with; "to rejoice" means to celebrate.

To accord with phenomena and principle without duality is to celebrate and rejoice without distinction between self and others. To accord with phenomena possesses the efficacy of skillful means (*upāya*);
to accord with principle possesses the virtue of reality (*bhūta*). To celebrate oneself possesses wisdom (*prajñā*); to celebrate others possesses compassion (*karuṇā*). Skillful means...

It is truly an obstruction. Because wisdom and compassion are equal, it is called "rejoicing" (*anumodana*). According to the present sutra, it is explained that one follows [the teaching] by diligently exhorting and instructing others in accordance with the doctrine;
this is the reason for "conformity. By imperial decree, he manifests his body to cause [others] to realize [the truth];

this is the reason for "joyful celebration. If even the Buddha rejoices, how much more so those of other vehicles! △ Second, receiving the mandate without contravention, in two parts: First, revealing the original vow.

At that time, the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, throughout immeasurable kalpas, I have constantly provided protection for sentient beings suffering in pain with a heart of loving-kindness and compassion; may you bear witness to this."
There are two kinds of suffering, three kinds of suffering, eight kinds of suffering, ten kinds of suffering, and so forth. "Embracing" (*yǒng*) refers to the physical body;

"protecting" (*hù*) refers to the mind and speech. Since beginningless kalpas, compassion has served as the internal primary cause, while sentient beings acting as protectors serve as the external conditions.
The Buddha’s three knowledges and five eyes have long since perceived this; yet, until one receives the Buddha’s command, [it remains unmanifest].
This is so even before receiving the teaching; how much more so after having received it! Therefore, it says, "I pray for realization.

The World-Honored One praised [Avalokiteśvara] in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*: "His great vows are as deep as the ocean; throughout inconceivable kalpas, merely hearing his name or seeing his body can extinguish all suffering of existence.
Mañjuśrī praised him in the *Śūraṅgama-samādhi-sūtra*: "Leaving suffering behind and attaining liberation—how excellent is Avalokiteśvara! Throughout kalpas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges..."
[He] enters into Buddha-lands as numerous as motes of dust, attains the power of great mastery, and fearlessly bestows gifts upon sentient beings. △ Second, clarifying the present mind:
For the sake of sentient beings, he preaches this *Yiqie Ruyi Lun* Dhāraṇī; if anyone receives and maintains it, they shall constantly perform their own work.
For those who recite with single-minded devotion, their aspirations shall be fulfilled. Now, receiving the Buddha’s majestic power, I thus rescue them from suffering.
"Karma" refers to the pure and wholesome karma; it denotes the body that performs the act of upholding [the teachings].
"Single-mindedness" refers to the mind. "Reciting" refers to the mouth. To "thus rescue from suffering" means to manifest the thirty-two responsive bodies.

It resides both within and without the burning house, rescuing and delivering all beings from the sufferings of birth-and-death, whether of the *pariccheda* (segmented) or *pariṇāma* (transformative) types.

It provides exhortation and instruction regarding the principles of practice for the five vehicles (*pañcayāna*). Its text contains three powers: first, the *dhāraṇī* mantra possesses majestic spiritual power.
Second is the power of accomplishing recitation through the chanting of pure karma; third is the power of gathering [beings] through the support of majestic vows.

The first and the last are powers from others, like a boat encountering a favorable wind; the middle is one's own power, like sails and oars. Furthermore, there are three ways of protective mindfulness:
first, protecting by manifesting one's own body to preach for sentient beings; second, protecting through the practitioner’s single-minded devotion...
The lower [part] refers to being able to receive protection; the third, "receiving majesty to save from suffering," refers to receiving empowerment and protection from above.
This clarifies that because the present mind is protected, it is needless to say that it will cause one to achieve the fruit of the Way. △ Third, the Section on Circulation.
At that time, having spoken this *Sūtra of the Wish-Fulfilling Wheel Dhāraṇī*, the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara,
the entire great assembly was filled with joy, and they all received it with faith and practiced accordingly.
The sovereign Bodhisattvas are able to explain the purity of persons; the dhāraṇī sūtras explain the purity of the Dharma;
and the great assembly attains the purity of the fruit through the joy of the Dharma. "All assemblies" refers to the fourfold assembly and the eight classes of beings.
Those who rejoice do so upon hearing its teachings; those who accept it with faith do so by contemplating its principles;
and those who practice it do so by cultivating its conduct. Thus, the three types of wisdom are fully developed, and the two benefits are equally accomplished.
That the mantras have been transmitted through successive kalpas and that the sūtra has spread throughout the Dharma-realm is a matter of necessity. This, too, was compiled by the sūtra-compilers.
